title: Review: Elements, monomers and condensation/hydrolysis; Monosaccharides and disaccharides; Polysaccharides; Food tests and chromatography; Lipids: triglycerides; Phospholipids, steroids and other lipids
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: BM04#t2 term and clue written for the game; BM06#t2 term and clue written for the game; BM09a#t1 term and clue written for the game; BM03#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BM02#N.8a, BM03#N.3, BM04#N.13a, BM05#N.3, BM06#N.4, BM09a#N.4a, BM09b#N.4, BM02#N.10a, BM03#N.10a, BM04#N.8, BM05#N.14, BM06#N.14. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Glycogen
items.clue: The energy store found in animals and fungi

items.label: Hydrophilic
items.clue: Describes the charged phosphate head, which interacts with water

items.label: Iodine test
items.clue: A change from orange-brown to blue-black shows that starch is present

items.label: Isomers
items.clue: Molecules such as glucose and fructose: same atoms, arranged differently

questions.stem: Two monosaccharides are joined by a condensation reaction to form a disaccharide. What happens in this reaction?

options.text: A molecule of water is taken in and split to supply the atoms that join the monomers
A covalent bond forms between the monomers and a molecule of water is released
A hydrogen bond forms between the two monomers, holding them together as a disaccharide
Water dissolves the two monomers so that they meet, but no water is formed or used

questions.explanation: An –OH from one monomer and an –H from the other combine to form water, leaving a covalent (glycosidic) bond between the monomers.

questions.stem: Two monosaccharides, P and Q, are drawn in their ring forms. In P the ring is made of four carbon atoms and one oxygen atom, with one further carbon atom (in a CH₂OH group) attached outside the ring. In Q the ring is also made of four carbon atoms and one oxygen atom, but two further carbon atoms (each in a CH₂OH group) are attached outside the ring. How should P and Q be classified?

options.text: Both P and Q are pentose sugars
Both P and Q are hexose sugars
P is a pentose and Q is a hexose
P and Q are alpha and beta glucose

questions.stem: Humans make amylase, which hydrolyses the 1,4-glycosidic bonds between α-glucose units in starch. Humans make no enzyme that hydrolyses cellulose, which also has 1,4-glycosidic bonds between glucose units. Which explanation is best?

options.text: Cellulose's glycosidic bonds are much stronger than those in starch, so amylase cannot break them.
Cellulose chains are coiled and branched, so amylase cannot reach the bonds.
Cellulose is non-polar, so it cannot dissolve and enzymes cannot act on it.
Its β-glucose units alternate in orientation, so its bonds have a different shape.

questions.explanation: Amylase only fits bonds between α-glucose units. In cellulose, alternate β-glucose units are flipped, so the bond looks different to an enzyme. Cows rely on gut microbes that make cellulase.

questions.stem: One glycerol molecule and three fatty acid molecules react by condensation to form one triglyceride. How much water is produced?

options.text: One water molecule is released
Three water molecules are released
Four water molecules are released
No water is released; water is used up

questions.explanation: Each –OH of glycerol reacts with the carboxyl group of one fatty acid in a separate condensation, forming an ester bond and releasing one water: three in total.

questions.stem: Which components are linked together by condensation reactions to form one phospholipid molecule?

options.text: One glycerol, two fatty acids and one phosphate group
One glycerol, three fatty acids and one phosphate group
Three glycerol molecules, one fatty acid and one phosphate group
Many fatty acid monomers joined in a chain, plus one phosphate group

questions.explanation: Glycerol has three hydroxyl groups. In a phospholipid two of them are linked by condensation to fatty acids and the third to a phosphate group, giving two hydrophobic tails and a hydrophilic head.

questions.stem: A solution gives a negative result with iodine. With Benedict's reagent, heated, it stays blue. A fresh sample is boiled with dilute hydrochloric acid, neutralised, and tested with Benedict's again: a brick-red precipitate forms. What does the solution contain?

options.text: A reducing sugar, because the final Benedict's test was positive.
Starch, which the acid broke down into glucose.
A non-reducing sugar, such as sucrose, and no reducing sugar.
A reducing sugar made by the acid joining smaller sugars by condensation.

questions.explanation: Negative first, positive after acid hydrolysis: the acid split a non-reducing sugar into reducing monosaccharides.

questions.stem: On a paper chromatogram of leaf pigments, the origin line was 20 mm from the bottom edge of the paper, the centre of the carotene spot was 65 mm from the bottom edge and the solvent front was 70 mm from the bottom edge. What is the Rf value of carotene?
questions.explanation: From the origin, the pigment moved 65 − 20 = 45 mm and the solvent front 70 − 20 = 50 mm. Rf = 45 ÷ 50 = 0.90.

questions.stem: A polypeptide made of 100 amino acids is completely hydrolysed into free amino acids. How many water molecules are used in the process?

options.text: 99 water molecules
100 water molecules
1 water molecule
0 water molecules

questions.explanation: 100 amino acids are joined by 99 peptide bonds. Each hydrolysis breaks one bond and uses one water molecule, split to supply the –H and –OH.

questions.stem: Galactose and glucose both have the formula C₆H₁₂O₆ and both form a ring of five carbons and one oxygen. They differ only in which way the –OH on carbon 4 points. Which statement is correct?

options.text: They are isomers: two hexoses with the same atoms arranged differently.
They must have different formulae, because they are different sugars.
They are α-glucose and β-glucose, the same sugar drawn in two different ways.
Galactose is a pentose, as only five carbons are in its ring.

questions.explanation: Same formula, different arrangement. Like glucose and fructose in the hook, that is enough to make a different sugar with a different shape.

questions.stem: Cellulose gives plant cell walls high tensile strength. Which feature of cellulose is responsible for this?

options.text: Straight chains lie side by side in bundles, cross-linked by many hydrogen bonds
The glycosidic bonds within cellulose are very much stronger than those within starch
The chains coil into tight helices that stretch and recoil like a spring
Beta-glucose is a larger monomer than alpha-glucose, giving thicker chains

questions.explanation: Straight, unbranched chains of β-glucose pack side by side in bundles linked by very many hydrogen bonds. Each is weak; together they resist stretching.

questions.stem: To make a spread, manufacturers react a liquid vegetable oil with hydrogen, using a catalyst. Some C=C double bonds in its fatty acid chains become C–C single bonds. How does the oil change?

options.text: It becomes more liquid, as double bonds stiffen chains and hold molecules together.
It becomes more unsaturated, as it now carries more hydrogen atoms.
It becomes more solid, as straighter chains pack more closely together.
It becomes more solid, as the extra bonds need more heat to break when it melts.

questions.explanation: Fewer kinks, closer packing, stronger attractions between molecules: a higher melting point. A liquid oil becomes a soft solid, like butter in the hook.

questions.stem: Lipoproteins carry cholesterol and triglycerides in blood plasma, which is mostly water. Each lipoprotein has an oily core of cholesterol and triglyceride, surrounded by a single layer of phospholipids (with some proteins). How are the phospholipids in this layer most likely arranged?

options.text: Tails facing outwards into the plasma; heads facing inwards into the oily core.
Heads facing outwards into the plasma; tails pointing inwards into the oily core.
Tails joined to one another by covalent bonds, forming a rigid shell around the core.
Mixed evenly through the oily core, as phospholipids are entirely hydrophobic like cholesterol.
